abstract:
Understanding the genetic regulation of metabolism is essential for improving animal health and productivity and for strengthening the use of pigs as translational models for human metabolic diseases. Metabolomics, when integrated with genomic data, provides a powerful framework for identifying genetic factors that influence intermediate molecular phenotypes closely linked to physiology. While large-scale metabolomics genome‑wide association studies (GWAS) have been extensively performed in humans, comparable studies in pigs remain limited. Among omics disciplines, metabolomics, the systematic study of metabolites central to physiology, represents the omics layer most closely linked to end-point phenotypes in mammals, such as health and production traits (e.g. growth rate). Metabolite levels are influenced by genetics, diet, and microbiome composition, with human studies showing high heritability and identifying numerous metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs). While such findings have advanced our understanding of disease biology in humans, comparable studies in pigs remain limited.
We performed GWAS of the serum metabolome in 213 three‑way crossbred pigs [(Landrace × Yorkshire) × Duroc], analyzing 248 metabolites and 30,628 metabolite ratios. We identified 41 significant metabolite-variant associations, which were consolidated into 18 mQTLs based on linkage disequilibrium (LD). Several regions were associated with multiple, biochemically related metabolites, while others showed highly specific effects. Cross-species comparison with the human GWAS catalog revealed candidate genes within seven mQTLs. Through an integrative prioritization strategy, putative causal genes-predominantly enzymes and transporters-were identified for 14 of 18 mQTLs.
Our results expand the catalog of genetic loci influencing serum metabolite variation in pigs and highlight both conserved and pig specific components of metabolic regulation. These findings provide a foundation for incorporating metabolomics into pig breeding programs and reinforce the value of pigs as a translational model for studying metabolite-associated traits and diseases in humans.
